reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: The infection and disease pattern in complement deficiency tracks the part of the cascade affected, so localising the defect predicts clinical risk

Deficiencies of the terminal components (C5-C9) and of properdin impair formation of the membrane attack complex and cause a striking susceptibility to recurrent Neisseria infection, especially meningococcal disease

Early classical-pathway deficiencies (C1q, C1r/s, C4, C2) predispose strongly to systemic lupus erythematosus and other immune-complex diseases because complement is needed to clear apoptotic cells and immune complexes
C3 deficiency, at the hub of all pathways, produces both severe pyogenic infection with encapsulated bacteria and immune-complex disease
Recurrent or unusual neisserial infection, or a single episode with an uncommon meningococcal serogroup, should prompt complement evaluation
The CH50 screens the classical pathway and the AH50 the alternative pathway; a near-absent total haemolytic complement points to a specific component deficiency to be confirmed by individual assays
Prevention centres on vaccination against encapsulated organisms-meningococcus (including serogroup B), pneumococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae type b-with prompt treatment of febrile illness
C1-inhibitor deficiency is a distinct entity causing bradykinin-mediated hereditary angioedema rather than the infection-prone phenotypes of other complement defects
Acquired complement consumption from active immune-complex disease must be distinguished from inherited deficiency, since low levels may simply reflect ongoing disease activity
reference.pathophysiology: The complement system comprises the classical, lectin, and alternative pathways that converge on C3 and the terminal pathway that assembles the C5b-9 membrane attack complex. Its functions include opsonisation, chemotaxis and inflammation, direct lysis of certain pathogens, and clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris. Inherited deficiency of a component removes the corresponding function: loss of early classical components impairs immune-complex handling and predisposes to lupus-like autoimmunity; deficiency of C3 or opsonic components causes pyogenic infection with encapsulated bacteria; and deficiency of terminal components or properdin cripples membrane-attack-complex killing of Neisseria. Regulatory-protein defects produce different phenotypes, such as C1-inhibitor deficiency causing angioedema and factor H/I defects causing atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Asplenia or hyposplenism with encapsulated-organism infection
Antibody deficiencies (e.g. CVID, specific antibody deficiency)
Acquired complement consumption from active autoimmune or immune-complex disease
Systemic lupus erythematosus and other connective-tissue diseases
Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome from complement-regulatory defects
additionalInvestigations: CH50 (classical pathway) and AH50 (alternative pathway) functional screens
Individual complement component assays to identify the specific deficiency
C3, C4, and C1q levels, distinguishing inherited deficiency from consumption
Autoimmune serology (e.g. ANA, dsDNA) when immune-complex disease is suspected
Genetic testing in selected or familial cases
Microbiologic confirmation and serogrouping of neisserial and other invasive infections
redFlags: Meningococcal or other invasive neisserial infection, or meningitis with rapid deterioration, requiring emergency antibiotics
Recurrent invasive infection with encapsulated bacteria signalling significant deficiency
Sepsis in a known complement-deficient or asplenic patient
Features of severe systemic lupus with major organ involvement in early-component deficiency
reference.prognosis: With appropriate vaccination, prompt treatment of infection, and in some cases antibiotic prophylaxis, most patients with complement deficiency do well. Prognosis is worse when invasive infection is not recognised early, and outcomes in early-component deficiency are additionally shaped by the severity of associated autoimmune disease.
pitfalls: Failing to evaluate complement after recurrent or unusual neisserial infection
Interpreting a low complement level as inherited deficiency when it reflects consumption by active disease
Neglecting to give and update the full schedule of vaccines against encapsulated organisms
Confusing C1-inhibitor deficiency (angioedema) with the infection-prone complement defects
management: Immunise thoroughly against encapsulated organisms, with particular emphasis on the full meningococcal programme (quadrivalent conjugate and serogroup B vaccines) in terminal-pathway and properdin deficiency
Treat infections promptly with appropriate antibiotics and consider antibiotic prophylaxis in those with recurrent neisserial disease
Give patients a written plan and a low threshold for urgent assessment of febrile illness, with empirical treatment for suspected meningococcal sepsis
Manage the systemic lupus erythematosus and immune-complex disease associated with early classical-pathway deficiency using standard immunosuppression
Localise the specific defect with functional screens and component assays, since the pattern of risk and management follows the part of the cascade affected
Provide genetic counselling and screen relatives once an inherited deficiency is confirmed
